Core explanation · 00:00–04:59

We will continue with module three on phase equilibria and in today's class we are going to learn how to construct a phase diagram of a two component system in general and specifically the lead silver system.

Key details

  • Then we study the determination of solid liquid equilibria and finally the Patterson's process.
  • When we talk of a two component system, we know that we need to use the phase rule F is equal to C minus P plus 1, which is known as the reduced phase rule.

  • F is equal to c minus p plus one.
  • And now out of pressure, temperature and composition, since pressure is being maintained constant, and especially for solid liquid equilibria, pressure is chosen constant variable.
  • When we are drawing this phase diagram of a two component system, this particular phase diagram will be known as a simple eutectic system.
  • One temperature scale stands for pure A and the other temperature scale stands for pure B.
  • And on the x axis we have the composition scale.
  • What is happening is here we have 100% A and as we move along this axis we are adding B into A.
  • of various compositions which are represented by A and B, the percentage of A and B.
  • Now the first thing we need to know is the melting point of pure A.
  • Now that melting point because this axis represents pure A and the temperature scale.
  • the alphabet M.
  • Now as we go on adding B into A, the we are actually adding an impurity into the pure substance A, and therefore we know that there is going to be a depression in freezing point.
  • When we add a certain amount of B, say a small amount of B, we find that it reduces the freezing point of pure A.
  • And as we go on adding more and more of A, we find that this goes on decreasing like this.
  • So therefore if I have to join these points I get a plot like this.
  • And now if I add A into the pure B again I will notice that there is a decrease in the melting point and if I join these again I get a line like this.
  • If I join these two they happen to meet at a point which is known as the utectic point.
